title.en: Apet the Great Mother: Life Came from Death, Light from Darkness
title.zh: 大母神阿佩特：死生於死，光生於暗

region.en: Thebes and Ombos, Egypt (the hippopotamus Mother of the gods)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯與翁博斯（河馬大母神）

texts.period: Theban lunar theology, pre-Hyksos; retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, the Apet theology

summary.en: The oldest Theban creation theology: Ah is the son of the great Mother deity Apet, identified with the female hippopotamus Taurt, goddess of maternity and mother of the gods; at Thebes and Ombos Osiris was regarded as the son of the sacred hippopotamus; at the beginning there was naught save darkness and water — the spirit of the night was the Great Mother, and her first-born was the moon child: life came from death and light from darkness.
summary.zh: 底比斯最古之創世神學：月神阿為大母神阿佩特之子——她被認同於雌河馬陶爾特，孕育之神、眾神之母；底比斯與翁博斯則以奧西里斯為聖河馬之子；太初唯有暗與水——夜之靈即大母，其長子為月之子：死生於死，光生於暗。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Theban theology retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling. The Apet-Taurt identification is Mackenzie's synthesis.

passages.text: It is highly probable that Ah was the son of the great Mother deity Apet, who was identified with the female hippopotamus Taurt, the mighty one, goddess of maternity, and mother of the gods. At Thebes and Ombos, Osiris was regarded as the son of the sacred hippopotamus. As we have seen in the Introduction, he was, like Ah, identified with the moon spirit, which symbolized the male principle. The Apet hippopotamus was the animal incarnation of the Great Mother; as a water goddess, therefore, Apet links with Nut, who rose from the primordial deep and was the waters above the firmament.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, with the retelling's quoted epithets rendered as plain text.

passages.text: At the beginning there was naught save darkness and water. The spirit of the night was the Great Mother, and her first-born was the moon child. Life came from death and light from darkness. Such appears to have been the conception of the worshippers of the sky-and-water goddess and the lunar god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII.

passages.text: As moon worship was of greater antiquity in Egypt than sun worship, and was associated with agricultural rites, the Theban cult must have made popular appeal, and helped to rally the mass of the people to throw off the yoke of the Hyksos Ra and Sutekh worshippers. The political significance of Apepa's order to slay the hippopotami is therefore apparent.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII, referring to the Hyksos king's order in the Apophis-Seqenenre tale tradition.

title.en: Amon the Husband of His Mother: The Hidden God Becomes King

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (the rise of the Amon cult)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（阿蒙祭之興）

texts.period: Theban theology of the 18th-20th Dynasties; retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, Amon the God of Empire

summary.en: How the lunar god of Thebes became Egypt's great father: Amon was originally the son of Mut-Apet, a moon-spirit traverser of space like Khonsu-Thoth who kept his lunar crescent even in hawk-headed form; as a Great Father deity, Amon, husband of his mother, became king of the gods and lost his original lunar character; his fusion with Ra was accomplished for political purposes — yet a Theban hymn still hails him in Memphis: Memphis receives thee in the form of Ptah, he who is the first-born of all gods.
summary.zh: 底比斯月神如何成為埃及偉父：阿蒙本為穆特-阿佩特之子，如孔蘇-托特般遍行之月靈，縱為鷹首仍戴月弦；大父神阿蒙既為母之夫，遂為諸神之王而失其月性；其與拉之融合乃為政治而成——然底比斯頌猶云：孟菲斯以卜塔之形迎爾——眾神之首生者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theology retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: As we have already suggested, it is possible that Amon was originally the son of Mut-Apet. He may have developed as a symbolized attribute of Ah. Fragments of old hymns make reference to him as a lunar deity, and as a traverser of space like Khonsu-Thoth. Indeed, even in his hawk-headed form, he retains his early association with the moon, for he wears the solar disk with the lunar crescent.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII.

passages.text: As a Great Father deity, Amon, husband of his mother, became king of the gods, and lost his original lunar character. His fusion with the sun god of Heliopolis, which was accomplished for political purposes, made the change complete, for he became Amon-Ra, the great representative deity of Egypt, who combines the attributes of all other gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII.

passages.text: As a god of war he rose into great prominence during the Eighteenth Dynasty. The victorious kings, who became owners of all the land in Egypt, and returned with great spoils from many battlefields, were lavish in their gifts to his temple, and his priests became exceedingly wealthy and powerful. There never was in Egypt a more influential cult than that of Amon-Ra.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII.

passages.text: At Memphis Amon-Ra was worshipped as Ptah. In a hymn addressed to the great Theban deity it was declared: Memphis receives thee in the form of Ptah, He who is the first-born of all gods, He who was at the beginning.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XXII, quoting the hymn to the Theban god.

title.en: The Deified Royal Couple: Ahmes-Nefertari and Amenhotep I
title.zh: 封神之王室伉儷：阿赫梅西-奈菲爾塔莉與阿蒙霍特普一世

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (the royal cult of the founders of the 18th Dynasty)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（第十八王朝開國者之王室祭）

texts.period: Cult from the 18th Dynasty onward (c. 1500-1100 BCE); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, the deified royal founders

summary.en: Kings who became protecting gods: the great Pharaohs were the religious Pharaohs — if a monarch was assiduous in venerating the gods, and especially in erecting and endowing temples, his fame was assured, for the grateful priests kept his memory green; Amenhotep I and his wife Aahmes-Nefertari were, after their death, revered as deities, protectors and punishers of men in the next world.
summary.zh: 成神之王：埃及所頌者乃虔敬之法老——王者若勤於敬神、建廟賜產，其名必不朽，感恩之祭司使其記憶常青；阿蒙霍特普一世及其妻阿赫梅西-奈菲爾塔莉死後受拜為神，為冥界之護者與罰者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal cult retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Although Ahmes I was the liberator of Egypt, his memory was not revered so greatly as that of his son and successor Amenhotep I (Amenophis). The great Pharaohs of the records were the religious Pharaohs; if a monarch was assiduous in venerating the gods, and especially in erecting and endowing temples, his fame was assured; the grateful priests kept his memory green. Amenhotep I and his wife Aahmes-Nefertari were, after their death, revered as deities; references are made to them as protectors and punishers of men in the next world.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XXII, with the retelling's quoted phrase rendered as plain text.

title.en: Osiris the Ancestor-god: From the Family Table to All Egypt
title.zh: 祖神奧西里斯：自家祭之席至全國之神

region.en: Egyptian tombs and stelae, from the Old Kingdom false doors onward
region.zh: 埃及陵墓與石碑（自古王國假門以降）

texts.period: Stele development Old Kingdom to 19th Dynasty (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911, ch. IX)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. IX, Osiris the Ancestral Spirit and God

summary.en: Why the dead man's stele stopped showing the dead man: the Old Kingdom false door shows the deceased seated at his offering-table, venerated as an ancestor who has attained to the life of the gods, a divine patron of his family; but under the 12th Dynasty the gods take the upper part of the stone, and by the 18th Osiris occupies the place of honour while the deceased is relegated to a corner — because, Budge argues, Osiris began as the ancestor-god of a small community and was adopted, town by town, until he became the ancestor-god of the whole country, exactly as African peoples elevate a chosen hero to be tribal ancestor.
summary.zh: 亡者之碑何以不再現亡者：古王國假門上，亡者坐於供案之側，如得神壽之祖宗受拜，乃家族之神護；至十二王朝，神像漸據碑首；至十八王朝奧西里斯居尊位而亡者退於一隅——伯奇論曰：奧西里斯本一小社群之祖神，城鎮逐一奉之，終為全國之祖神——恰如非洲諸族擇一英雄立為部落之祖。

sensitivity.note: Ancient iconographic argument via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. The African parallels (Barotse, Shilluk) are Budge's comparative evidence.

passages.text: The deceased sits in state, and we see him venerated as an ancestor who has attained to the life of the gods; he is, in fact, a divine patron of his family to whom petitions for help can be addressed in time of need.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. IX.

passages.text: On a great many stelae of this period Osiris occupies the place of honour, and the figure of the deceased is relegated to a corner. From the above facts it is clear that the figure of Osiris, or Osiris Khenti-Amenti, usurped the place occupied in stelae of the Ancient Empire by the deceased. Up to the time when the cult of Osiris spread throughout Egypt, the Egyptians, I believe, worshipped their ancestors, according to the custom of the African in most parts of the Sudan, then and now.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. IX.

passages.text: Everything about the figure of Osiris suggests that in one aspect at least he was an ancestor-god, probably at first of a comparatively small community. As the cult of the god spread, town and village communities all over Egypt adopted him as their ancestor-god, par excellence, and little by little he became the ancestor-god of the whole country.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. IX.

passages.text: The Shilluks were in the habit of selecting a particular hero from among the dead, and they constituted him the ancestor of their tribe; when they needed rain or a good harvest they called upon him by name to provide it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. IX, the comparative African evidence.

texts.canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (London, 1911), ch. IX

narrative.en:
Every Egyptian tomb of the Old Kingdom confronts the visitor with a false door, and carved or painted on the stone a man seated at his meal: the deceased on a four-legged African stool, a table of bread, beer, oil, wine, geese and legs of beef before him, his wife sometimes beside him, and around the walls reliefs of family and servants carrying offerings for the funerary commemorative service held daily or at intervals. The dead man sits in state, venerated as an ancestor who has attained to the life of the gods — a divine patron of his family to whom petitions for help can be addressed in time of need. This is the everyday theology of African ancestor worship, cut in limestone.

Budge's chapter tracks what happened to that man on his own stone. Under the Middle Kingdom, gods begin to share the stele: on one 12th-Dynasty stone the king's cartouche stands at the top with Khenti-Amenti and Ap-uat beside it; on another, Isis and Horus set up the pole bearing the head-box of Osiris, the cow-headed Hathor behind them, and the kneeling owner of the tomb is pushed to the margin. Under the 18th Dynasty the figure of Osiris is usually sculptured on the upper part of the stone, the deceased below him in a subordinate position; on many stones Osiris occupies the place of honour and the figure of the deceased is relegated to a corner. Under the 19th Dynasty the upper field fills with Amen-Ra Ka-mut-f in ithyphallic form, with the foreign goddesses Anthat and Kent, Mut and Khensu, and groups of solar boats.

Budge's reading is that the stone records a social revolution in theology. Before the Osiris cult spread, Egyptians worshipped their ancestors, according to the custom of the African in most parts of the Sudan, then and now; everything about the figure of Osiris suggests that in one aspect at least he was an ancestor-god, probably at first of a comparatively small community. As the cult spread, town and village communities all over Egypt adopted him as their ancestor-god, par excellence, and little by little he became the ancestor-god of the whole country — which explains why at Abydos, the central city of his cult, the stelae of strangers are crowded with his figure. The mechanism is not Egyptian alone: the Barotse divine with knuckle-bones whether an ancestor is displeased and sacrifice grain and honey at the grave; the Shilluk select a particular hero from among the dead and constitute him the ancestor of their tribe, calling on him by name for rain and harvest. Osiris is Egypt's selected hero — the dead king who rose — promoted from one family's table to the national table of offerings.

functions: Documentary evolution of ancestor worship into state god: the stele sequence as theology in stone
Family religion: the deceased as divine patron to whom petitions are addressed in time of need
Comparative ethnology: Osiris' rise explained through African hero-elevation customs (Barotse, Shilluk)

title.en: The Shabtiu: Servants for the Celestial Corvee
title.zh: 沙伯提俑：天界勞役之僕

region.en: Egyptian tombs, 6th Dynasty to the Roman Period
region.zh: 埃及陵墓（第六王朝至羅馬時期）

texts.period: Shabti figures from the 6th Dynasty onward, inscribed from the 12th (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911, ch. VI)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. VI, the Shabtiu figures

summary.en: The worker-figures buried with the dead: the Shabti is a figure of stone, alabaster, wood or faience found in tombs from the 6th Dynasty to the Roman Period, mummy-shaped at first, later with hands crossed, then each hand holding an ankh, later a hoe, and last of all a basket thrown over the shoulder; the inscribed text is identical with the 6th Chapter of the Book of the Dead and calls the figure, in the dead man's name, to perform his labours in the Other World — tilling, planting, watering the fields, bringing sand from the East to the West; and Maspero's explanation, Budge argues, is the right one: the earliest uninscribed figures represent the slaves who were buried with their masters.
summary.zh: 與死者同葬之工人俑：沙伯提俑以石、雪花石膏、木、彩陶等製成，自第六王朝至羅馬時期見於墓葬——初為無手木乃伊形，繼而交手於胸，再各執安卡、後持鋤，末則肩荷筐籃；其銘文即《亡靈書》第六章，以亡者之名呼其俑代行冥界之勞——耕種灌田、自東運沙至西；馬斯佩羅之解最確：古之無銘者，乃代殉葬之僕。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary practice via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Maspero's retainer-sacrifice reading links the shabti to the funeral-murders evidence.

passages.text: The Shabti, or Shauabti, is a figure made of stone, alabaster, wood, faience, etc., and is found in tombs from the VIth dynasty to the Roman Period. In the VIth dynasty the Shabti appears to have been uninscribed; in the XIIth it frequently bears the name and titles of the person for whom it was made, and with whom it was buried; and in the XVIIIth and following dynasties, in addition to the name and titles of the deceased, it bears a text which is identical with the VIth Chapter of the Book of the Dead. Its earliest form is that of a mummy with no hands showing, later it has its hands crossed over the breast, later each hand holds the emblem of life, still later each hand holds a hoe, and last of all a basket is thrown over the shoulder.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. VI.

passages.text: The text, which is cut or written on figures from the XIIth dynasty onwards, explains quite clearly the purpose which the figures were intended to serve, for in it the figure is called upon, in the name of the deceased person written upon it, to perform whatsoever labours he might be adjudged to do in the Other World. These labours consisted in tilling and planting and watering the fields, and in bringing sand from the East to the West, and in doing whatsoever had to be done in connection with agriculture in the Other World.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI.

passages.text: The custom of burying mummy-figures of this kind with the dead seems to be senseless unless we accept the view which we owe first of all to Professor Maspero, viz., that they represent the slaves who were buried, alive or dead, with their masters, in order that their spirits might serve the spirits of their masters in the Other World, just as their bodies had ministered to their masters' bodies in this world.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. VI, citing Maspero's reading of the retainer burials.

title.en: The Monolith That Refused to Move: The Artificer's Groan
title.zh: 不欲行之巨石：匠人之嘆

region.en: Sais, Egypt (the temple of Athene/Neit, before whose door the colossus lies)
region.zh: 埃及薩伊斯（雅典娜/奈特神廟，巨構臥於門前）

texts.period: Reign of Amasis (26th Dynasty, 570-526 BCE); recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.175 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 175

summary.en: The stopped colossus of Sais: Amasis dedicated a chamber of one single stone, hauled from Elephantine by river, twenty days' journey, by two thousand chosen men of the boatmen class, three years in the work — but while the house was being drawn along the chief artificer groaned aloud, seeing that much time had been spent and he was wearied by the work, and Amasis took it to heart as a warning and did not allow them to draw it further onwards; so it stands outside the temple gate, and some say a man was crushed under it.
summary.zh: 薩伊斯之停運巨構：阿馬西斯以整石鑿室，自象島由水路運來、程二十日，用二千選自舟子階層者、工歷三年——然室行之際，主匠大聲而嘆，嘆工程之久、其身之疲，王以為警，遂止而不令再運——故其室立於廟門之外；一說有槓夫壓死於石下，故亦不復內運。

sensitivity.note: Ancient prodigy-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Amasis also dedicated in Sais the chamber of the temple of Athene, which is over against the entrance; it is of the length of one-and-twenty cubits, and the breadth fourteen cubits, made of one single stone... the stone was brought from the town of Elephantine by the river, a distance of twenty days' journey: and the matter of the transport was the work of two thousand chosen men allotted to the class of boatmen, and this class of men had this business in charge for three years.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.175.

passages.text: This lies by the side of the entrance to the temple; for within the temple they did not draw it, because, as it said, while the house was being drawn along, the chief artificer of it groaned aloud, seeing that much time had been spent and he was wearied by the work; and Amasis took it to heart as a warning and did not allow them to draw it further onwards. Some say on the other hand that a man was killed by it, of those who were heaving it with levers, and that it was not drawn in for that reason.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.175.

title.en: Declare Your Livelihood: The Law Solon Took from Egypt
title.zh: 申爾生計：梭倫自埃及取回之法

region.en: Egypt under Amasis and Naucratis, the Greek trading city
region.zh: 阿馬西斯治下之埃及與希臘商城諾克拉提斯

texts.period: Reign of Amasis (570-526 BCE); recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.177-178 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 177-178

summary.en: The lawgiver's debt to Egypt: in Amasis' reign Egypt flourished as never before, and it was Amasis who established the law that every year each Egyptian should declare to the ruler of his district from what source he got his livelihood, on pain of death — and Solon the Athenian received from Egypt this law and had it enacted for the Athenians.
summary.zh: 立法者之埃及師承：阿馬西斯之世，埃及之盛冠絕往昔——王立法定制：凡埃及人歲告其州長以何術謀生，違者處死——雅典人梭倫自埃及得此法而頒行之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient legal-history tradition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the reign of Amasis it is said that Egypt became more prosperous than at any other time before, both in regard to that which comes to the land from the river and in regard to that which comes from the land to its inhabitants, and that at this time the inhabited towns in it numbered in all twenty thousand. It was Amasis too who established the law that every year each one of the Egyptians should declare to the ruler of his district, from what source he got his livelihood, and if any man did not do this or did not make declaration of an honest way of living, he should be punished with death.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.177.

passages.text: Now Solon the Athenian received from Egypt this law and had it enacted for the Athenians, and they have continued to observe it, since it is a law with which none can find fault.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.177.
